The graph above shows $y=k{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}+c.$  Find the value of $k-c.$
worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote of the curve $y=k{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}+c$ is $y=c.$ In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=-3,$ hence $c=-3.$

We can solve for $k$ by finding a point on the graph and substituting for $x$ and $y.$ The labeled point on the graph is $(0,3),$ so we substitute $x=0$ and $y=3$ into the function and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}k{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}+c & =y \\ k{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}-3 & =y \\ k{(\frac{1}{2})}^{0}-3 & =3 \\ k-3 & =3 \\ k & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
k-c=6-(-3)=9.
$$

The equation of the curve is $y=6{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}-3.$
